item.title: [Critical] A PRC-linked crew took credentials and secrets from a renewable operator’s own code server and left its SSH keys behind
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit published findings on 13 September, picked up by The Hacker News on 14 September and Industrial Cyber on 15 September. It describes a campaign it attributes, with moderate confidence, to Red Heron, an actor operating in a PRC-linked context. The vehicle is CVE-2026-60004, a CVSS 9.8 remote code execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea, fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July. Acronis says the operator began building tooling within days of the 28 July advisory and had scanned 1,386 Gitea instances across seven countries by 30 July. It confirms 11 compromised targets in five countries: Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka. The Hacker News’ headline figure of 13 organisations in six countries does not match the primary report, so this page uses Acronis’ count. CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August with a federal remediation deadline of 28 August, now long passed. Two of the victims are why this leads the page. From a Taiwanese industrial-automation company the actor took repositories for a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments. It also took a surveillance and monitoring product, IoT platform integrations, a network sniffer and server configurations. At a Canadian renewable-energy operator, Acronis counts 22 separate exploitation sessions. The actor took source code, credentials and secrets, mapped the operator’s Docker networks, and planted its own SSH keys in authorized_keys for persistent access. The tooling includes an implant Acronis tracks as JITTERLY, with more than 30 post-exploitation commands, and an LD_PRELOAD Linux rootkit it calls SIXZUT. Be precise about what this is and is not. It is a confirmed compromise of an electricity-sector organisation by an actor a vendor assesses as PRC-linked. It is not a government attribution, and it is not confirmed manipulation of generation or grid control; nothing in the reporting says a plant moved. But what the actor took and left behind at the Canadian operator is what you would want if you intended to come back: credentials and secrets that authenticate to the estate, a map of how it is networked, and SSH keys that survive a password reset. No public statement says remediation is complete, and no new development was reported between 17 and 21 September. - Acronis Threat Research Unit analysis of 13 Sep 2026 (primary, re-read 21 Sep 2026) — reported by The Hacker News on 14 Sep 2026 and Industrial Cyber on 15 Sep 2026; CVE, CVSS and KEV detail from the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue - Gitea fix 27 Jul 2026; advisory 28 Jul 2026; scan of 1,386 instances complete by 30 Jul 2026; KEV addition 25 Aug 2026 (due 28 Aug, passed); campaign reporting 13–15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Clusters exploiting Cisco firewall management consoles include one with Sandworm-overlapping tooling and a Qilin ransomware affiliate — and Cisco’s hardening release has now shipped
item.category: Incident — Exploited firewall management platform, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. It is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three post-compromise clusters. UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 and is not attributed to a named actor. UAT-11823 used CVE-2026-20079 together with CVE-2026-20316 and delivered Cyclops Blink malware; Talos describes “overlaps in tooling with the Sandworm APT actor”, which is not an attribution to Sandworm. UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence is a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a CVSS 5.3 static-credential flaw that is not in KEV, then carried out reconnaissance, stole credentials and built a list of endpoints to target for encryption. On 16 September Cisco published its hardening release, cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN, covering eight internally found flaws across ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9); it accompanies the exploited FMC flaws. No OT impact and no utility victim has been named. But FMC is the console that configures the firewalls enforcing the boundary between your corporate network and generation, substation and DER control networks, and the tooling overlap Talos describes is with Sandworm, the actor with the longest record of causing electricity outages. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek, with cluster detail corroborated by The Hacker News - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; federal deadline 12 Sep 2026; hardening release 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Fire Ant turns Cisco routers and TACACS servers into listening posts inside critical-infrastructure networks
item.category: Incident — Network and authentication tier compromise
item.description: Sygnia published findings on 30 August that the China-nexus group it tracks as Fire Ant has moved past VMware hypervisors into the network layer itself, compromising Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts inside a large interconnected environment. On the routers it ran an implant that suppressed selected syslog messages, opened outbound sessions and served interactive shells with no logging. On TACACS it injected a library into the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as sessions were accepted. Sygnia says the group used that position to scan and attempt connections into linked critical-infrastructure networks, without confirming compromise there. For an electricity operator the uncomfortable part is the ordering: routers and TACACS are what your control-centre audit trail rests on, so if they are lying, every downstream log inherits the lie. - Sygnia research publication and press release — corroborated by BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Cybersecurity Dive and SC Media - Sygnia published 30 Aug 2026; wider reporting 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — electric and gas delivery not affected
item.category: Incident — Confirmed customer-data breach at an electric and gas utility
item.description: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based utility serving about seven million customers in Texas, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio, said in an SEC Form 8-K filed on 14 September that an unauthorised third party obtained customer personal information through one of its external-facing systems. It found out after someone posted online claiming to hold the data. The company says electric and gas delivery has not been impacted and it does not expect a material financial effect; it has brought in outside experts and notified law enforcement and regulators. The actor claims about 7.49 million records — names, addresses, account and billing data and partial Social Security numbers — taken by abusing a public API with no rate limiting, and has leaked a 2.5 GB archive. BleepingComputer puts the intrusion window at roughly 17 August to 1 September. Neither CenterPoint nor SecurityWeek has verified the record count. The actor also threatened to “attack the main infrastructure” next time; that is an unverified claim, and nothing reported links this breach to operational systems. The point for other operators is the entry route: a customer-facing API belongs to the utility’s attack surface as much as a VPN does. - CenterPoint Energy Form 8-K filed with the SEC — reported by BleepingComputer, The Record and SecurityWeek - 8-K filed 14 Sep 2026; reporting 15 Sep 2026; intrusion window about 17 Aug–1 Sep 2026 per BleepingComputer

item.title: [Medium] A Bavarian municipal utility’s IT was encrypted and supply kept running — then it warned customers their bank details may be exposed
item.category: Incident — Municipal utility IT encrypted, supply unaffected
item.description: Stadtwerke Landsberg in Bavaria says attackers encrypted its central IT systems overnight into 1 September in what it calls a targeted criminal cyberattack. Its press release, posted 3 September under the heading “rebuild under way”, and reporting by The Record citing the utility say electricity, water and other essential services kept running, while phone and email contact was limited. On 7 September the utility posted a GDPR Article 34 notice to affected people saying it could not rule out access to or theft of customer data, including names, addresses, contact details and bank details. No ransomware group has claimed the attack, no extortion demand is known, and no newer statement or recovery-complete notice had appeared as of 16 September. It is the pattern that keeps recurring at smaller utilities: the business network goes down, supply holds, and the lasting damage is data exposure and recovery time — an outcome that depends on the separation between IT and operations actually holding. - Stadtwerke Landsberg press releases and GDPR notice — reported by The Record - Attack about 1 Sep 2026; press release posted 3 Sep 2026; GDPR notice 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Berlin refused to pay, and the published dump reportedly includes critical-infrastructure vulnerability analyses
item.category: Incident — Government breach exposes critical-infrastructure risk documentation
item.description: Rhysida released the data it took from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set runs to roughly 5.79 TB across about 1.44 million files and, alongside personnel and payroll records, is reported to contain vulnerability analyses covering the city’s water supply plus plaintext credentials for municipal systems including a building atlas, a payments database and administrator accounts. The city’s own account has data leaving from 7 August and continuing to around 12 August, with the affected departments not physically disconnected until 14 August. For a utility the transferable point is not the ransomware — it is that the documents which describe how to hurt you frequently sit somewhere you do not control: with a regulator, a municipal owner, an engineering consultancy or an interconnection partner. - Berlin state administration statements — reported by Help Net Security and Security Affairs - Breach and refusal to pay reported 1 Sep 2026; data published by the actor 4 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing, and the sector detail is worth more than the headline. Utility victims doubled from five in July to ten in August, the sharpest proportional rise of any category, while Qilin alone accounted for 157 claims, roughly a quarter of the month. The named utility victims in the same tracking fit that shape: the Italian water utility Alto Calore Servizi, listed by the Titan group, and Grayson Rural Electric Cooperative, listed by Qilin on 2 September with claims of service disruption and data theft. Both are leak-site claims rather than victim confirmations, and neither organisation nor CISA has acknowledged them. Qilin has made a habit of small US electric cooperatives, having claimed two Texas co-ops in late 2025, which points at the real pattern — distribution utilities without a 24-hour security operation rather than investor-owned utilities with mature monitoring. The operational lesson from this year's utility incidents is consistent: the encryption lands on the business side, and the outage — billing, dispatch support, work management, customer service — follows from IT dependence rather than from anything touching a relay. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For the power sector this is familiar ground — the idea grew out of national-lab work on grid consequence — but the argument has sharpened: design decisions, not detection tooling, determine whether a compromised network becomes a physical event. Protection schemes, interlocks and non-digital trip paths are security controls. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Exposed PLCs and flat remote access at small US electric utilities draw fresh vendor attention
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector exposure
item.description: Reporting on 15 September covered a vendor push specifically aimed at the exposed-PLC and remote-access problem facing small US water and electric utilities — the gap that has driven federal warnings all summer. Small municipal and cooperative electric utilities carry the same exposed-controller and flat-remote-access problem that the summer’s water-sector attacks exploited, without the staff to fix it. The underlying facts are the ones that matter and they are already federally documented: the FBI and EPA warned on 30 July that actors were reaching internet-facing Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs at water and wastewater utilities, changing IP addresses and passwords, and causing loss of view and in some cases loss of control, with reported effects including pressure loss and flooding. A subsequent internet-wide scan reported by CyberScoop found roughly 4,400 exposed programmable logic controllers still reachable, including 22 in cities that had recently been attacked. Vendor marketing aside, the exposure is real, measured and unresolved. - FBI and EPA public service announcement of 30 July 2026, CyberScoop exposure scan reporting, and vendor coverage via Industrial Cyber - FBI/EPA PSA 30 Jul 2026; vendor coverage 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] DOE and Sandia put a language model on the least glamorous part of grid detection: preparing the data
item.category: Research — AI-assisted grid threat detection
item.description: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response and Sandia National Laboratories reported on 8 September on C2E2, a tool developed under the AI-FORTS programme that uses large language models to automate the data-engineering step in cyber-physical threat detection for the electric grid. The point is not that a model spots the attack. It is that turning heterogeneous SCADA, relay, PMU and network telemetry into a form a detection model can consume normally takes a specialist roughly two months per deployment; Sandia reports cutting that to hours, with around 95% accuracy in detecting and localising simulated threats in testing. That matters for utilities because data preparation, not algorithm choice, is what has stalled most anomaly-detection projects at the pilot stage. Sandia is clear this has not yet been trialled at an operating utility, and the next phase specifically targets hallucination-driven false or missed detections — a failure mode a control room cannot tolerate. - DOE CESER and Sandia National Laboratories, reported by Industrial Cyber - Reported 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The campaign that hit water is now probing energy control systems — and there is a $10 million bounty attached to it
item.category: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact
item.description: Reporting on 2 September said Iranian government-linked operators have widened their targeting beyond the water sector to telecommunications networks and energy providers, concentrating on internet-exposed automated control systems. Officials quoted describe attempted intrusions rather than confirmed operational impact so far, and that distinction is worth holding on to. Separately, on 3 September the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on an IRGC-affiliated figure it links to the campaign against US critical infrastructure. For a generation or transmission operator the useful detail is the access pattern rather than the actor: the water intrusions ran through controllers and cellular-connected devices reachable from the public internet with weak or default authentication, not through any novel exploit. The equivalent exposure here is unmanned substations, remote generation and DER sites, and standing vendor maintenance links. - NBC News reporting on the widened targeting and the State Department Rewards for Justice announcement as carried by The Record — water-campaign scale from CISA guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement - Widened-targeting report 2 Sep 2026; reward announced and reported 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
item.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a utility the honest question is what your detection-to-containment interval actually is between the corporate boundary and the control centre, and whether it survives an adversary working at machine pace overnight. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] GRIDLOCK: modelling puts a 92% chance of a major attack on UK battery storage by 2031 — and 29% of the fleet is enough
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Scenario modelling
item.description: Centrii published its GRIDLOCK report on 3 September, modelling what happens when an adversary uses grid-connected battery storage as the weapon rather than the target. In the scenario, compromised BESS units are commanded to swing output in concert, manipulating physical power flows to destabilise system frequency rather than saturating a network link — the report frames it as a grid-scale denial of service delivered in energy. Across 10,000 Monte Carlo runs against three security postures, Centrii puts the probability of a major attack on UK battery storage by 2031 at 92%, and calculates that compromising roughly 29% of national capacity — on the order of 400 units — could be enough to trigger a nationwide outage affecting 67 million people, with costs modelled up to £10 billion. Mandatory certification and regular attack-readiness drills cut that probability to 61% and push the earliest likely window from 2027 to 2028. A parallel run on Texas returns the same 92% figure by 2031, with economic damage modelled up to $65 billion. This is modelling rather than a reported incident, and its value is in the premise it tests: a large amount of fast-acting capacity dispatched from a small number of control planes. - Centrii GRIDLOCK report — reported by Industrial Cyber and New Civil Engineer - Published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six steps to being able to disconnect — and a planning horizon of three months running islanded
item.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
item.description: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. The step that changes the engineering is the second-to-last one — keeping monitoring alive after you cut the link, since an isolation plan that also blinds the control room is not one anyone will execute. The addition worth arguing about internally is the planning horizon: Nozomi suggests operators assume they may need to sustain isolated operations for up to three months. For generation and transmission that pushes the question past network design and into spares, licence servers, time synchronisation and how long an EMS can run without its enterprise dependencies. - Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance - Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

item.title: [Medium] A hostile battery dispatch looks identical to a profitable one — and very few control planes can order it
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Analysis
item.description: Help Net Security published an analysis on 2 September, built on modelling from Rafael Narezzi of the London firm Centrii, arguing that grid-connected battery energy storage has concentrated an unusual amount of fast-acting power behind a small number of cloud control planes. Batteries earn revenue by responding to frequency in under a second, so on a control room screen a hostile coordinated swing and a legitimate revenue-driven one look the same — the frequency trace alone tells the operator nothing about intent. Control is also pooled: third-party optimisers and manufacturer cloud platforms dispatch fleets spread across many sites and several balancing areas, which means the meaningful unit of risk is the platform, not the individual site. This is analysis and modelling rather than a reported incident, and it is worth reading as a design question about who can issue a fleet-wide setpoint and what would notice if someone else did. - Help Net Security interview and analysis with Centrii - Published 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Researchers used an AI model to port a working PLC exploit to a second controller — then bricked it
item.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. The honest read for a utility is narrow but real: this does not create new exploits, it lowers the cost of spreading an existing one across the model variants sitting in your substations and generating sites. - Forescout Vedere Labs research reported by SecurityWeek - Reported 1 Sep 2026; underlying flaw CVE-2021-31886 disclosed 2021

item.title: [Critical] NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating that it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that the activity has resulted in some limited real-world disruption. It names no victims, actors or techniques. What makes it worth reading in a control room is the framing: the NCSC tells organisations not to assume their OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. For an electricity operator that is a direct description of the embedded generation, storage and unmanned substation estate — the sites commissioned by an integrator, connected over a carrier link, and never re-surveyed. It lands three days after DESNZ confirmed a UK generator was taken offline by a cyberattack. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026; the NCSC says it has been engaging affected sectors directly ahead of publication

item.title: [High] One crafted network message can stop an ABB Freelance DCS controller
item.category: Advisory — Process DCS controller denial of service, vendor PSIRT
item.description: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a flaw reserved in 2023 and published only now. It is an improper handling of a length-parameter inconsistency: a specially crafted message sent to the controller makes it stop, and the attacker needs no credentials, only network reach to the controller. ABB’s machine-readable advisory rates it CVSS v3.1 7.5. Affected are Freelance DCP, AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier, 2013 SP1, 2016, 2016 SP1, 2019 and 2019 SP1. The fixes already ship in existing update rollups — 2013 SP1 RU06 or later, 2016 SP1 RU07 or later, 2019 SP1 RU03 or later and 2019 SP1 FP1 — and Freelance 2024 is not affected. ABB reports no exploitation and no prior public disclosure. Editorial assessment: Freelance is ABB’s process DCS, and where it runs a generating station’s auxiliary or balance-of-plant systems, a stop-the-controller condition reachable from the control network is exactly the kind of flaw that matters. Many sites run long-lived releases that never took the later rollups, so being on a supported version is not the same as being fixed. - ABB cybersecurity advisory 7PAA010706 (CSAF), listed on ABB’s cybersecurity alerts index; CVSS v3.1 7.5 per the CSAF file, although ABB’s index shows a different score - Advisory and CVE record published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA adds three exploited Linux kernel flaws to KEV — the kernel inside a lot of substation and plant edge gear
item.category: Advisory — Confirmed exploited, CISA KEV, Linux kernel
item.description: On 18 September CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September — three days, and that date has now arrived with no exploitation detail published since the listing. CVE-2025-39682 is in the kernel TLS receive path and is reported as CVSS 9.8; CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in the ebtables SNAT target on systems with bridge netfilter rules, reported as 8.8; CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface, reported as 7.8. These are local, post-access flaws — the step that turns a foothold on a Linux host into root — not remote entry points. No detail has been published on who is exploiting them or against what, and no OT vendor, product or sector has been named. None of the CVEs from CISA’s 17 September ICS advisories is among them. Editorial assessment: Linux runs historians, jump hosts, SCADA front-end servers, substation gateways and much industrial edge hardware, and vendor firmware typically trails upstream kernel fixes by months. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue (version 2026.09.18) and CISA alerts of 18 Sep 2026 — reported by The Hacker News; CVSS scores as reported by outlets - KEV additions 18 Sep 2026; reporting 19 Sep 2026; federal deadline 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] ABB closed a password-reset takeover in its dynovaPRO energy-asset cloud — after spotting suspicious resets at nine customers
item.category: Advisory — Cloud energy-asset management, account takeover
item.description: ABB published advisory 4JDE002044 on 17 September for CVE-2026-18963, rated CVSS v3.1 9.1, in dynovaPRO, ABB’s cloud system for managing energy assets such as EV chargers, batteries and photovoltaic systems. The flaw sits in the Keycloak authentication component built into the platform: an unauthenticated attacker could force the password-reset flow for any user without clicking the email verification link, which amounts to account takeover. ABB fixed it on its own side on 27 August, so customers have nothing to install, and it disabled password reset for all customers as an interim measure. ABB says the CVE was publicly disclosed on 17 August, roughly ten days before the cloud fix. ABB says it had not received confirmed reports of active exploitation as of 27 August, but its own analysis found 26 password-change events across nine customers that it treats as possible testing or reconnaissance, and it disabled those accounts. That is suspicious activity observed by the vendor, not confirmed exploitation. Editorial assessment: an account on a platform like this can change how chargers, batteries and PV behave at a site, so a takeover is a control-plane question for DER and storage owners, not only a data-exposure one. - ABB cybersecurity advisory 4JDE002044 (CSAF, revision A), listed on ABB’s cybersecurity alerts index - Advisory published 17 Sep 2026; server-side fix 27 Aug 2026; public CVE disclosure 17 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco ISE is being exploited — and ISE is what decides who gets onto your OT network
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited zero-day, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC: an API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco’s PSIRT states it is aware of active exploitation. All versions of ISE and ISE-PIC are affected; the fixed releases are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September — three days, which is as short as that clock gets. That deadline has now passed, and no new advisory revision or exploitation reporting appeared over the 19–21 September weekend. There are no workarounds; short of patching, Cisco’s only mitigation is restricting management traffic with infrastructure ACLs. No actor attribution has been published, the only hunting guidance is to review access logs for unfamiliar usernames, and no targeting of industrial or critical-infrastructure operators has been claimed. The reason it belongs on this page is structural rather than sectoral: in most utilities ISE is the NAC and 802.1X policy engine that authorises switch ports, issues certificates and gates the remote-access paths into the industrial DMZ. Administrative control of that policy engine is administrative control of who is permitted to be on the control network, and a quiet policy change there will not look like an attack in anyone’s console. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue — reported by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek - Cisco advisory published and KEV listing added 16 Sep 2026; fixed-version detail reported 17 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 19 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A crafted email is enough to run commands as root on Cisco’s Secure Email Gateway
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited zero-day, CISA KEV
item.description: CVE-2026-76461 is a SQL-injection flaw in the AsyncOS email-parsing path of the Cisco Secure Email Gateway, rated CVSS 9.8. An unauthenticated attacker who sends a message carrying malicious SQL statements can reach arbitrary command execution with root privileges, with no user interaction. Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX on 14 September and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation during September; CISA added the CVE to the KEV catalogue the same day, 14 September, with a federal remediation deadline of 17 September. Both physical and virtual appliances are affected regardless of configuration, and Shadowserver counted more than 400 appliances exposed to the internet. Cisco names 16.5.0-780 as the preferred fixed release alongside fixed builds in the 15.5 and 16.0 lines; take the exact build strings from the Cisco advisory, because the outlets covering this disagree on them. Researchers quoted by Cybersecurity Dive note that on-premises gateways carry more pivot risk than cloud-hosted instances and that the flaw would suit a state-linked espionage operation. No critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed and no attribution has been published. For a utility this is an initial-access item rather than an OT one: the mail gateway is a permanently internet-facing appliance inside the corporate estate that talks to directory services, and root on it is a well-worn first step towards the engineering network. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive, BleepingComputer and Help Net Security - Cisco advisory published and KEV listing added 14 Sep 2026; federal deadline 17 Sep 2026; attack-vector detail reported 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 17 September batch reaches a transmission FACTS controller and an industrial edge platform
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisory release, 17 September
item.description: CISA published seven ICS advisories on Thursday 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07. They cover Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric’s Modicon M340 controller and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (models 750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The one that matters most to this audience is Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, which controls transmission-level flexible AC transmission equipment. Per reporting on the Hitachi Energy advisory, the platform is exposed through its embedded GWS component and inherits five 2024 CVEs first disclosed for MicroSCADA/MACH GWS: CVE-2024-4872 and CVE-2024-3980, both rated CVSS 9.9; CVE-2024-7940, rated 8.3, a service exposed on all interfaces without authentication and the one to lead with for network exposure; CVE-2024-3982, rated 8.2; and CVE-2024-7941, rated 4.3. Affected are FACTS Control Platform versions 3.4.0 through 4.1.1 where the GWS component is installed. Outlets disagree on whether a fixed release exists, so take remediation from Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229 rather than assuming a patch. ABB Ability Edgenius 3.2.0.0 to 3.2.4.0, an industrial edge platform found in utility and process environments, is affected by the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” flaw CVE-2026-31431 (CVSS 7.8), fixed in 3.2.4.1. The Modicon M340 advisory is a CISA republication of a 2025 Schneider advisory: CVE-2025-6625, a denial of service via crafted FTP commands rated 7.5 under CVSS v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, fixed in firmware SV3.70. NetBotz 5 carries CVE-2026-13336 (6.4 under v3.1, 7.3 under v4.0) and CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0; PowerChute Serial Shutdown carries CVE-2026-13348 (5.3 under v3.1, 6.9 under v4.0), an excessive-authentication-attempts flaw, with version 1.6 as the fix. The Mitsubishi advisory covers CVE-2026-15688, an authentication-algorithm flaw rated 8.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, affecting all versions and described as permitting local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs. The Bransys ELD advisory covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential issues, the highest rated 7.5, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch. Separately, ICSA-26-211-07 on Mitsubishi’s CC-Link IE TSN communication protocol was updated on 17 September, adding eight affected products and removing three. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -07, tracked through the cisagov CSAF repository; CVE and CVSS detail for -01 and -04 to -07 from the CISA CSAF files; Hitachi Energy FACTS CVE detail per ISSSource and WindowsForum reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229 - Advisories published 17 Sep 2026; ICSA-26-211-07 updated 17 Sep 2026; Hitachi Energy reporting 18 Sep 2026; the Mitsubishi and Hitachi advisory files were not in the CSAF mirror at generation time

item.title: [Medium] Secure Lock credentials on Schneider’s SCADAPack x70 RTUs are not protected well enough
item.category: Advisory — Remote terminal units, credential protection
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-04, published 15 September and republishing Schneider Electric’s SEVD-2026-251-03 of 8 September, covers CVE-2026-81861 — insufficiently protected credentials in the Secure Lock feature of the SCADAPack x70 range, rated CVSS v3 6.5 and 5.9 under CVSS v4. The listed products are the SCADAPack 47x, 47xi, 47xd, 470R and 57x, with the product tree also naming the SCADAPack 3xx and 32. The consequence is unauthorised access to RTU configuration. Schneider lists no firmware fix in the advisory; the published remedy is configuration work — enable role-based access control as described in the SCADAPack security guidelines, segment the network, and use the RTU Firewall Service to restrict which services answer. No exploitation is reported. On a power system these are the RTUs behind distribution automation, recloser and capacitor-bank control, and remote telemetry, and they usually live at unmanned sites reached over a cellular or radio link. That is precisely the population that ends up outside the segmentation an operator believes is in place, which is what turns a medium-severity configuration flaw into an access-path problem. - CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-04, republishing Schneider Electric security notification SEVD-2026-251-03 of 8 Sep 2026 - Vendor advisory 8 Sep 2026; CISA republication 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and grid and generation teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. For a utility this is not a developer problem. Self-hosted GitLab is where many transmission and generation operators keep substation automation configs, EMS/SCADA integration scripts, relay setting files, DER management code and the credentials that tie them together. Unauthenticated file reads against that server hand an attacker the engineering keys to a CIP-scoped estate without ever touching a relay. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi finishes its SCALANCE LPE9403 work: twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device
item.category: Research — Vendor-patched OT edge device, chainable to root
item.description: Two dates on this item have been reported loosely elsewhere, so take them first. Nozomi Networks Labs’ PROFINET DCP research — four memory-corruption flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403, tracked as CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578 and each rated CVSS 5.3 for denial of service — was published on 10 September, and those CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18. What happened on 15 September was CISA updating that advisory to version 4 to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes; it was not a new critical advisory. On 18 September Nozomi published the second part of the research, and that is the part worth acting on. It describes twelve vulnerabilities in total — nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client — reported with CVSS scores ranging from 5.3 to 8.5. Affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and the Edge Client up to and including V2.1; both are fixed in V4.0 HF0 and later, and Siemens has published an advisory and patches. Nozomi says several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onto adjacent networks. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. In a substation or generation estate the LPE9403 is the box between the process bus and everything above it, aggregating data for EMS, historians or cloud analytics — so root on it means the numbers your control room trusts can be edited before they arrive, which is a harder problem to notice than the device going offline. - Nozomi Networks Labs research of 10 and 18 Sep 2026 and Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438, with CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Original CVE disclosure May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18; PROFINET DCP research 10 Sep 2026; CISA advisory update to v4 on 15 Sep 2026; second research publication 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Siemens patches an authentication bypass in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays, the gear that trips your feeders
item.category: Critical Advisory — Protection relay, no known exploitation
item.description: Siemens ProductCERT published SSA-142885 on 8 September, covering fourteen vulnerabilities in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relay family across every firmware version before V2.70. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS 9.8, is an information disclosure in the device web interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker calculate current and previous session identifiers and step straight past authentication. Two companion issues make that worse: weak session-token entropy in CVE-2026-62646, and a role-based access control bypass in CVE-2026-62650 that hands an attacker administrative rights. A pre-authentication denial-of-service condition is also fixed. Siemens reports no exploitation, and no change of state was found when the advisory was re-checked on 11 September. This remains the highest-consequence unexploited item on the board for transmission and distribution operators because of placement rather than score — 7SR5 relays sit in feeder, transformer and busbar protection schemes, and Siemens took the unusual step of reminding TSOs and DSOs to confirm their redundant secondary protection is healthy. Update, 15 September: CISA republished the advisory as ICSA-26-258-05, listing CVE-2026-62645 as missing authentication for a critical function and again reporting no known public exploitation. The same CISA release updated its Siemens SICAM 8 advisory (ICSA-26-197-05, fixes in V26.20) and its Siemens products-using-OpenSSL advisory (ICSA-26-174-03, CVE-2025-15467), and republished Schneider Electric’s SCADAPack x70 credential-protection flaw CVE-2026-81861 as ICSA-26-258-04. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 and CISA republication ICSA-26-258-05 — corroborated by SecurityWeek’s September ICS Patch Tuesday round-up - Published 8 Sep 2026 (v1.0); CISA republication 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] mySCADA myPRO Manager carries a CVSS 9.8 missing-authorisation flaw that exposes privileged management functions and the SMS modem behind them
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA management software, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September for mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. CVE-2026-73807, a missing-authorisation flaw scored CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567, missing authentication for a critical function scored 6.3, could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a connected GSM modem. mySCADA fixes both in version 2.2. CISA lists Energy among the affected sectors, alongside critical manufacturing, food and agriculture, transportation and water, and reports no known public exploitation. For power teams the exposure is most likely at smaller or remote sites where a web-managed SCADA package and SMS alarm notification are in use; an attacker able to send texts through that modem can also undermine trust in the alarms operators rely on. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03 - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] “MikroTrick” moves from disclosed to confirmed exploited — two CVSS 9.2 SSH flaws hand over RouterOS admin
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick” — disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited — is now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors; it noted only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. That is the honest boundary of this item — there is no confirmed utility victim and no confirmed OT impact. It earns a place here because of where this hardware tends to live in an electricity network: cheap, capable routers are a common choice for cellular or fixed-wireless backhaul at unmanned substations, distributed generation sites and storage compounds, often installed by a contractor and often the one device on that site with a route to both the corporate network and the RTU. - CERT Polska alert — reported by Industrial Cyber. No victims or sectors named; no confirmed OT impact - Exploitation observed from 2 Sep 2026; CERT Polska confirmation 9 Sep 2026; CISA KEV listing 12 Sep 2026, federal deadline 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Dutch NCSC warns exploitation of two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws is imminent — patches landed 9 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent
item.description: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre issued a warning reported on 12 September that it expects near-term exploitation attempts against two critical vulnerabilities in Check Point VPN products, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both carrying CVSS 9.8 in reporting. The pair can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can additionally affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. No public proof-of-concept code had been reported in the coverage at the time of the warning, and no exploitation has been confirmed — the NCSC’s position is a forecast, not an observation, and it should be read that way. It matters to electricity operators because the Check Point gateway is frequently the device terminating third-party and vendor access into the utility environment: relay and SCADA vendors, protection contractors, DER aggregators and the remote-engineering paths that reach substation and generation networks all tend to land on the same estate of gateways. - Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning — reported by BleepingComputer. Assessed as imminent; no confirmed exploitation and no named victims - Check Point fixes released 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning reported 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Check Point patches a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication root flaw in the server that writes your IT/OT boundary policy
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management server, unauthenticated RCE
item.description: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, a CVSS 9.8 stack overflow in the login process of its Security Management and Log Servers, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and SecurityWeek on 18 September from vendor advisory sk1000155. An unauthenticated request carrying an overly long username can lead to remote code execution as root. Multi-Domain Server is also affected; Smart-1 Cloud has already been fixed on the vendor side. Affected on-premises lines include R82.10 up to JHF Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, R81.20 up to Take 166 and R81.10 up to Take 190, plus the end-of-support R81 and R80.x; for R82.20, reporting says no protective hotfix take exists yet across its builds. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition — that detail could not be checked against the vendor text, so do not rely on it to rule yourself out. Check Point says it has “no indication” of exploitation in the wild. This is a different flaw from the VPN pair the Dutch NCSC flagged on 12 September, but it lands on the same estate: at many utilities the Check Point management server is what defines the rules on the firewalls separating corporate IT from generation, substation and control-centre networks, so control of it is control of that boundary. - Check Point advisory sk1000155 — reported by The Hacker News and SecurityWeek; the vendor page itself could not be retrieved for this edition. No named victims and no confirmed exploitation - Reported 17 Sep 2026 (The Hacker News); SecurityWeek round-up 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including the remote-support tool your integrator probably uses
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-support and build tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September after evidence of active exploitation, setting federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to obtain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload; and the RouterOS entry reflects the CERT Polska chain covered separately on this page. For a utility the ScreenConnect entry is the one to read twice. Remote-support and RMM tooling is how integrators, protection contractors and OEM support desks reach engineering workstations and HMIs, and it is frequently installed outside the asset inventory the security team maintains. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13, 14 and 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA’s 8 September KEV batch is led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your MSP uses
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor fixes already available. The one that matters most to utilities is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection weakness giving pre-authentication remote code execution on the remote monitoring and management server. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline was 11 September and has now passed. RMM platforms are a recurring bridge into OT-adjacent networks at MSP-managed generating stations, substations and DER sites, because the agent runs with high privilege on the very hosts that reach engineering systems. The batch also carries two exploited Windows privilege-escalation zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026 — corroborated by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and CyberScoop reporting on the N-able and Microsoft disclosures - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships nine advisories, Schneider four, with a distribution RTU fix in the pile
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday
item.description: The 8 September ICS patch round landed heavier than usual for electricity operators. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven of them on the day, with critical findings in the Reyrolle 7SR5 relay family covered separately above, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT, and began rolling out fixes for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8 across affected product lines. Schneider Electric published four. The most severe is a critical authentication vulnerability in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2. Closer to the grid edge, Schneider also fixed a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300 — the former Easergy T300 RTU used for MV feeder automation and substation remote terminal duty — alongside EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert and a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Aveva disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA published them on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: CVE-2026-81821, a hardcoded cryptographic key, and CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing, both at CVSS 8.4, alongside a missing-authorisation issue at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, all fixed in Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited, and that remained true when the batch was re-checked on 11 September. The T300 item is covered separately below. - Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric and Aveva security advisories of 8 Sep 2026, plus CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 of 10 Sep 2026 — summarised by SecurityWeek and ISSSource - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026; Aveva advisory published by CISA 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The one genuinely new power item this cycle is a feeder-automation RTU — Schneider’s PowerLogic T300
item.category: Advisory — Distribution feeder RTU, no known exploitation
item.description: Schneider Electric’s September 2026 patch release included a high-severity vulnerability in the PowerLogic T300 platform, the rebranded Easergy T300 remote terminal unit used for MV distribution feeder automation and monitoring. It is a separate advisory from the Modicon M580 critical flaw (CVE-2026-3869) and the Siemens Reyrolle 7SR5 relay set published in the same cycle, and it is the only genuinely new electricity-sector disclosure found in the 9–11 September window. Be clear about what is and is not known: the secondary reporting reviewed — SecurityWeek’s ICS Patch Tuesday round-up and the associated conference coverage — characterised the severity only as “high” and did not carry a CVE identifier or a CVSS vector, so none is published here. A vendor fix or mitigation was issued as part of the same September advisory cycle. No exploitation has been reported. The reason it matters out of proportion to a missing score is the device’s job: a T300 sits in a ring main unit or pole-mounted cabinet and actuates switchgear, so it is one of the few products in this month’s pile that can directly change the state of a distribution feeder. - Schneider Electric September 2026 advisory cycle — reported by SecurityWeek’s ICS Patch Tuesday round-up. CVE identifier and CVSS vector not disclosed in the secondary reporting reviewed - Vendor cycle 8 Sep 2026; reporting 9 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch lands on remote access and the firmware tool — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform
item.description: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September. Three are worth an operator’s attention. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 lets an attacker achieve remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — that machine is usually an engineer’s laptop or a jump host that already holds a route into substation and plant networks. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 allows commands or code to run at the permission level of the logged-in user; ControlFLASH is the tool used to push firmware to relays, controllers and communication modules, so the account running it is normally privileged. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects — relevant wherever Ignition fronts an EMS or generation SCADA layer. None is reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-02 (IXON VPN Client), ICSA-26-246-03 (Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH) and ICSA-26-246-06 (Inductive Automation Ignition) - Published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos - Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch available
item.description: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through ICSA-26-244-05, published 1 Sep 2026, cross-checked against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index - Advisories published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition and the PaperCut security bulletin — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security, Rapid7 and The Hacker News - Vendor disclosed active exploitation 27 Aug 2026; CVEs assigned 28 Aug 2026; added to KEV 31 Aug 2026; post-exploitation activity reported by Arctic Wolf 6 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A protocol test set that talks directly to your field devices picks up two flaws — one of them a decade old
item.category: Advisory — Protocol test set used on DNP3 and IEC 60870 links
item.description: CISA’s 27 August advisory batch includes ASE2000 V2, the communications test set engineers use to exercise DNP3, IEC 60870-5 and Modbus links when commissioning or troubleshooting RTUs, relays and substation gateways. Two issues are documented in versions 2.25 through 2.37: a bundled Apache log4net component that does not disable XML external entities when parsing its configuration file (CVE-2018-1285), and improper certificate validation in 2.35 through 2.37 (CVE-2026-18717) that lets an attacker on the path impersonate the trusted peer, complete the TLS handshake and read or alter the protected traffic. The reason this belongs on a power page rather than in the noise is placement, not score: the test set runs on a laptop that is deliberately connected straight to protection and control equipment, often inside the substation fence, and it is exactly the kind of tool that travels between sites. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-239-04, published in the 27 Aug 2026 batch of seven advisories — corroborated by the WaterISAC weekly roundup - Published 27 Aug 2026; verified 30 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
item.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
item.description: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is an ICS product, and all three sit in the layer utilities depend on rather than the layer they regulate. The Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-53362 matters because the historian, engineering server, protocol gateway and network monitoring appliance in most substations and control centres are Linux underneath, and vendor appliances inherit kernel patches on the vendor’s schedule rather than yours. CVE-2026-66384 in JFrog Artifactory is a path-traversal issue in a build-artifact repository — relevant where firmware, HMI images or automation packages are staged before they reach the field. The ownCloud bug, CVE-2023-49105, is nearly three years old and patched, which usually means the exposed instances are ones nobody owns. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition, corroborated by Security Affairs and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; ownCloud flaw originally disclosed Nov 2023

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from “patch soon” to confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. The flaw is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August, following publication of a technical analysis and proof of concept. Federal agencies must remediate by 29 August. For utilities, NetScaler frequently fronts the remote access that engineering, control-centre and vendor staff use to reach OT. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor advisory and patches released August 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026; continued exploitation reported 5 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] FERC approves CIP-014-4: one 36-month cycle, jointly owned facilities in scope, and a 1,500-foot look around the fence
item.category: Policy — NERC reliability standard, transmission physical security
item.description: FERC has approved NERC reliability standard CIP-014-4, published in the Federal Register on 15 September under section 215 of the Federal Power Act and reported by Industrial Cyber the following day. The standard governs how transmission owners identify and assess the stations and substations whose loss could result in instability, uncontrolled separation or cascading. Four changes matter operationally. Applicability now extends to jointly owned transmission facilities. The previous 30-month and 60-month cycles are consolidated into a single 36-calendar-month review and assessment cycle, aligned with TPL-001 planning. Risk assessments must use steady-state and dynamic simulations across peak and off-peak load cases. And the assessment must consider stations and substations within 1,500 feet, about 457 metres, of the facility in question. The effective date is 1 October 2028, and FERC estimates roughly 344 transmission owners in scope at about ten hours a year each. It follows the 2022 substation attacks and FERC’s December 2022 directive to evaluate CIP-014-3. This is physical security rather than cyber — but the identification step is shared work, because the same station list drives CIP-002 classification, and a facility that changes status under one standard tends to change it under the other. - FERC order approving NERC CIP-014-4, Federal Register publication of 15 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber - Federal Register publication 15 Sep 2026; reporting 16 Sep 2026; standard effective 1 Oct 2028

item.title: [Info] CISA makes the case for decoys — and OT is the one place where adding a fake asset is easier than changing a real one
item.category: Guidance — Detection and response for critical infrastructure
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence or support the collection of threat intelligence, and it structures deployment across three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions the technique alongside zero trust as an incremental, low-disruption detection measure rather than a replacement for controls. It reads better in an OT context than in an IT one for a simple reason: the standard objection to new detection in a control environment is that touching a production system carries risk, and a decoy does not touch one. A fake historian, a spare engineering workstation that is not actually used, or a honeytoken credential seeded on a jump host changes nothing in the process. And because legitimate traffic inside a control network is narrow and predictable, a single interaction with a decoy is a far higher-quality alert than most of what a utility SOC currently spends its day triaging. The cost is maintenance: a decoy that stops matching the estate around it becomes obvious to an attacker and useless to you. - CISA guide “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Guidance published and reported 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether your patch process quietly depends on it
item.category: Policy — Vulnerability-management data source
item.description: CISA will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin from 28 September, SecurityWeek reported on 17 September, directing users instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, alerts and advisories. The agency frames the change as consistent with Binding Operational Directive 26-04 of June 2026 and its shift towards risk-based prioritisation. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. The practical question for a utility is procedural rather than technical. The weekly summary is a common input to vulnerability-management routines and, in more than a few programmes, it is the documented patch source named in the evidence trail kept for NERC CIP-007 patch-management obligations. If a procedure of yours points at that bulletin, the source needs changing before the end of the month, and the change itself needs recording. KEV and the ICS advisory feed are the obvious replacements, with one caveat worth stating in the procedure: KEV is deliberately narrower, listing only what is known to be exploited, so a programme that swaps one for the other without adjusting its criteria will quietly stop tracking a great deal it used to see. - CISA notice of retirement of the weekly Vulnerability Summary — reported by SecurityWeek - Reported 17 Sep 2026; bulletin retired 28 Sep 2026; BOD 26-04 issued June 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. For a utility the CRA is mostly a procurement lever rather than a direct obligation: it is your relay, RTU, inverter and gateway vendors who now carry the reporting duty, and their disclosures are about to become more timely and more visible. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] DOE names Frenos, Raptor Dynamix and Bastazo under its SENTRY energy cybersecurity programme
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Federal funding programme
item.description: The US Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) announced on 14 September three recipients under its Securing ENergy Technology ResiliencY (SENTRY) programme, which runs through ConnectWerx. Frenos is building AI-driven adversary emulation for energy-sector attack scenarios; Raptor Dynamix is developing a counter-drone system for utilities it calls Grid Guardian; and Bastazo is building a cyber-informed engineering risk-quantification framework. DOE did not publish award amounts. The relevance to an operator is less the awards than what they signal about where federal attention in grid security is going: adversary emulation against energy environments, drones as a physical threat to utility sites, and engineering-led risk quantification. It sits alongside the Department’s request for industry input on bulk-power equipment and supply-chain risk, and is reported here factually, without comment on the policy direction. - US Department of Energy CESER SENTRY award announcement — also reported by Industrial Cyber - Announced 14 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] DOE has opened the comment window that decides what grid-equipment provenance will actually mean
item.category: Policy — Bulk-power system supply chain, comment period open
item.description: The Department of Energy published a Request for Information in the Federal Register on 9 September implementing the executive order of 26 August that declared a national emergency over bulk-power-system security. The RFI asks industry for input on foreign ownership and control, equipment provenance, firmware and software integrity, and remote-access practices for grid-connected equipment, naming inverters, battery energy storage, uninterruptible power supplies, generators and industrial control systems. Comments are due 9 October 2026, and DOE held its public webinar on 16 September. This is the mechanism that turns August’s order into procurement and compliance obligations, which makes a four-week window the only inexpensive opportunity to shape what those obligations look like in practice. The substantive point for an operator is that the questions DOE is asking — who manufactured this, what firmware is on it, and who can reach it remotely — are ones most CIP-013 supply-chain programmes cannot currently answer for inverter-based resources and storage, because that equipment usually arrives through an EPC contract rather than being bought directly. - US Department of Energy Request for Information published in the Federal Register — reported by Industrial Cyber, with legal analysis from Holland & Knight - Executive order 26 Aug 2026; RFI published 9 Sep 2026; public webinar 16 Sep 2026; comments due 9 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — 24 hours to tell ENISA about an exploited flaw
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, follow up within 72 hours with detail on the exploit and mitigation status, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available. They must also inform affected users. The regime reaches manufacturers placing products on the EU market regardless of where they are based, with penalties running to €15 million at the top of the scale. For a utility the practical effect is on the supply side rather than the compliance side: relay, RTU, EMS/SCADA, inverter and DER-platform vendors selling into Europe are now on a 24-hour clock, so exploitation-confirmed disclosures about grid equipment should surface faster and in a more standardised form than the sector is used to. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the first hours of an incident are when they collide
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting
