item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than ideological: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours when containment is most effective. Electricity operators recognise the shape of this — a single event at a registered entity can trigger E-ISAC reporting, an OE-417 to the Department of Energy, NERC CIP-008 obligations, state utility commission notification, and, for entities with federal contracts or regulated data, more besides. The analysis lands as CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn, which is the point at which harmonisation either happens or does not. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO data, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Medium] The free assessment small operators actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
item.category: Policy — CISA reported to be ending six free critical-infrastructure assessment services
item.description: Cybersecurity Dive reported on 3 September that CISA has told staff to stop delivering six of the free assessment services it has offered critical-infrastructure owners, including its on-site architecture design review and several facilitated risk and resilience assessments, following an internal direction reportedly given on 25 August. The agency had not published a formal notice as of this edition, so the exact scope and end dates should be read as reported rather than confirmed. The operators most affected are the ones with the least to fall back on: municipal utilities, generation and transmission co-operatives and small investor-owned utilities that used these engagements as their only external review, and for whom the commercial equivalent is a five-figure engagement not in this year’s budget. - Cybersecurity Dive reporting, carried by Utility Dive — based on an internal CISA meeting described by people familiar with it; no formal agency notice had been published as of this edition - Direction reportedly given 25 Aug 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] OpenAI pledges $1bn to put frontier AI in the hands of critical-infrastructure defenders — eligibility still undefined
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry initiative
item.description: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Detail on cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice has not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For electricity operators this is worth logging rather than acting on, but it lands in a telling week: Forescout published its demonstration that a supervised model can re-target a working PLC exploit at a sibling controller in a matter of hours, so capability is accumulating on both sides of the line. If your utility is small enough that a programme like this would change what tooling you can afford, register interest early — and settle two questions before committing anything operational to it: what leaves your environment, and what happens to the capability when the subsidy ends. - SecurityWeek reporting on OpenAI’s Daybreak announcement - Announced and reported 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance — and it applies to you as a service provider, not just to your suppliers
item.category: Policy — Joint international guidance, incident communications
item.description: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks providers to hold a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, to send plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, to give affected users root-cause and technical detail they can act on, and to align messaging with legal and regulatory duties. The framing is deliberately about service providers, which is how a utility should read it in two directions at once: it is the standard to hold your EMS, metering and remote-support vendors to, and it is also the standard your customers, your balancing authority and your regulator will apply to you during an outage you cannot immediately explain. - Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and CISA — joint guidance “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers” - Published 2 Sep 2026
